Locusts are not a separate kind of insect but certain species of grasshopper that can change dramatically in appearance and behavior. For years the two forms of the migratory locust were classified as different species. In 1921 the Russian-born entomologist Boris Uvarov proposed that they were in fact a single species, and that one form could turn into the other. He called the two forms phases: a solitarious phase, whose members are usually green and avoid one another, and a gregarious phase, whose members are more conspicuously colored, more active, and attracted to one another.

What causes the switch? Work on the desert locust in the 1990s and 2000s suggested that crowding itself is the trigger. When a period of good rains is followed by dry weather, the plants the insects feed on can shrink into small patches, and solitary locusts gathering there bump into one another. Researchers found that repeatedly touching the hind legs of a solitary locust for a few hours was enough to make it start behaving gregariously. A 2009 study linked this change to a rise in serotonin, a nervous-system chemical; blocking serotonin prevented the shift.

The behavioral change comes first, while the change in color and body shape can take more than one generation to complete. Once enough insects have shifted, they march together as wingless young and later fly in swarms, which can travel long distances and destroy crops along the way. Understanding the trigger has raised hopes of predicting outbreaks before swarms form.

In the late eighteenth century, many people in Europe assumed that Earth was only a few thousand years old. The Scottish thinker James Hutton disagreed. He argued that land is slowly worn down by rain and rivers, that the debris settles as layers of sediment on the sea floor, and that these layers are eventually hardened into rock and raised up to form new land. If such slow processes had built the landscape, he reasoned, the planet must be immensely old.

Hutton looked for evidence in places where two sets of rock layers meet. In 1788 he traveled by boat along the coast east of Edinburgh with two companions, the mathematician John Playfair and the geologist James Hall, and at a headland called Siccar Point they found what he had hoped for. There, layers of gray rock stand almost vertically, and on their worn edges lie layers of red sandstone tilted only gently. Such a break is now called an unconformity. To Hutton, it recorded a series of events: the lower layers had been deposited flat, pushed upright, and worn down before the sandstone was laid over them.

Each step in that series would have required an enormous span of time. Playfair later wrote that looking so far back made the mind seem to grow dizzy. Hutton could not say how old Earth was. Estimates in years came only in the twentieth century, when the radioactive decay of elements in rocks provided a way to measure geological ages.

By the early seventeenth century, well diggers and pump makers in Italy knew a curious fact: a suction pump could not raise water more than about ten meters. Galileo discussed the limit but did not settle the question. In 1644 his former assistant Evangelista Torricelli described an experiment that pointed to an answer. He filled a glass tube about a meter long and closed at one end with mercury, covered the open end, and turned the tube upside down into a dish of mercury. The mercury in the tube fell until its column stood roughly seventy-six centimeters high, leaving an empty-looking space above it.

Torricelli proposed that the column was held up not by any pull from the empty space but by the weight of the air pressing down on the mercury in the dish. Mercury is nearly fourteen times as dense as water, so the pressure that supports a column of mercury about seventy-six centimeters high would support a column of water roughly fourteen times taller, close to the limit the pump makers had found.

If the weight of the air held up the column, the column should be shorter where there was less air above it. In 1648 the French scholar Blaise Pascal asked his brother-in-law, Florin Périer, to carry the apparatus up the Puy de Dôme, a mountain in central France. At the summit the mercury stood several centimeters lower than at the base, as the idea predicted. The instrument came to be known as the barometer.

In the Trobriand Islands, off the eastern tip of New Guinea, the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski spent much of the period from 1915 to 1918 observing a system of exchange that he described in his 1922 book Argonauts of the Western Pacific. The system, called the kula, links communities on a ring of islands. Its objects are of two kinds: long necklaces of red shell discs and armbands of white shell. Necklaces travel around the ring in a clockwise direction and armbands counterclockwise, and a necklace is exchanged for an armband, never for another necklace.

What puzzled outside observers was that kula objects are not owned in the usual sense. A man who receives a famous necklace keeps it for a time, usually no more than a year or two, and then passes it on to a partner farther along the ring. The valuables have little practical use, and the armbands are said to be seldom worn except on special occasions. Yet men undertook long and sometimes dangerous voyages by canoe to obtain them. A man's standing came from the valuables that passed through his hands and from the partnerships he maintained, which could last a lifetime.

Malinowski noted that ordinary trade, in which useful goods were bargained over, took place alongside the kula, but he insisted that it was a separate activity. Later scholars, notably the French sociologist Marcel Mauss, drew on his account to argue that gifts which must be returned can bind people together in lasting obligations.

In 1970 the economist George Akerlof published a short paper about used cars, titled "The Market for 'Lemons'," now one of the most widely cited in economics. A "lemon" is American slang for a defective car. Akerlof's point was that the seller of a used car usually knows much more about its condition than any buyer can discover. Economists call such a situation asymmetric information.

Suppose buyers cannot tell good cars from lemons. They will then be willing to pay only a price that reflects average quality. But that price is too low for owners of good cars, who know their cars are worth more, so some of them withdraw from the market. The cars that remain for sale are, on average, worse, and buyers who anticipate this lower their offers further, which drives out still more good cars. At the extreme, the market could shrink until only lemons were traded, or until no trade took place at all, even though some buyers would gladly pay a fair price for a good car.

The argument applies well beyond cars. Health insurance is a common example: if an insurer cannot judge who is likely to fall ill, the customers most eager to buy at a given price may be those with the highest expected costs. Akerlof noted that markets develop ways to reduce the problem, such as guarantees, brand names, and licensing. In 2001 he shared the Nobel Prize in economics with Michael Spence and Joseph Stiglitz for this line of work.

In 1963 the ecologist Robert Paine began a simple experiment on a stretch of rocky shore at Makah Bay, on the Pacific coast of Washington State. Along this shore the ochre sea star preys on mussels, barnacles, and other animals that live attached to the rocks. On one section Paine pried the sea stars off by hand and threw them into deeper water, and he kept removing any that returned. A nearby section was left alone for comparison.

The results were striking. Without its main predator, the California mussel spread across the cleared rocks, crowding out and smothering other species. Within a few years the number of species there had fallen, by Paine's count, from fifteen to eight, while the untouched section changed little. Removing a single predator had made the community poorer, not richer, apparently because the sea star had been keeping the strongest competitor for space in check.

He borrowed the image of the wedge-shaped stone at the top of an arch that holds the other stones in place. The idea proved influential, and later researchers applied it to animals such as sea otters, which by eating sea urchins can protect kelp forests. Ecologists have also debated how widely the label should be used, since few species have been tested as directly as the ochre sea star.

Over the past few million years, Earth's climate has swung repeatedly between long glacial periods, when ice sheets covered much of North America and northern Europe, and shorter, warmer intervals like the present one. In the nineteenth century the Scottish scientist James Croll proposed that these swings were driven by slow changes in Earth's orbit. In the early twentieth century the Serbian engineer Milutin Milanković developed the idea much further, spending years calculating by hand how the sunlight reaching different latitudes had varied.

Milanković considered three cycles. The shape of Earth's orbit shifts from nearly circular to slightly elongated over roughly 100,000 years. The tilt of Earth's axis varies between about 22 and 24.5 degrees over about 41,000 years. And the axis slowly wobbles, changing the season in which Earth passes closest to the Sun over roughly 19,000 to 23,000 years. In his view, what mattered most was summer sunlight in the high northern latitudes. When summers there were cool, some of the winter's snow survived until the next winter, and over many centuries ice sheets could grow.

For decades the theory lacked a reliable test, because no one could date past climate changes precisely enough. That changed in 1976, when an analysis of deep-sea sediment cores found climate cycles matching all three periods. One puzzle remains. Over the last million years, glacial cycles have lasted about 100,000 years, yet the orbital change with that period has the smallest direct effect on sunlight. Why it dominates is still debated.

In the nineteenth century the Scottish scientist James Croll proposed that these swings were driven by slow changes in Earth's orbit. In the early twentieth century the Serbian engineer Milutin Milanković developed the idea much further, spending years calculating by hand how the sunlight reaching different latitudes had varied.

Milanković considered three cycles. The shape of Earth's orbit shifts from nearly circular to slightly elongated over roughly 100,000 years. The tilt of Earth's axis varies between about 22 and 24.5 degrees over about 41,000 years. And the axis slowly wobbles, changing the season in which Earth passes closest to the Sun over roughly 19,000 to 23,000 years. In his view, what mattered most was summer sunlight in the high northern latitudes. When summers there were cool, some of the winter's snow survived until the next winter, and over many centuries ice sheets could grow.

For decades the theory lacked a reliable test, because no one could date past climate changes precisely enough. That changed in 1976, when an analysis of deep-sea sediment cores found climate cycles matching all three periods. One puzzle remains. Over the last million years, glacial cycles have lasted about 100,000 years, yet the orbital change with that period has the smallest direct effect on sunlight. Why it dominates is still debated.

Until the middle of the twentieth century, most cargo crossed the oceans as what shippers called break-bulk freight: sacks, barrels, crates, and bales loaded one at a time. Teams of dockworkers carried each item from a warehouse or truck to the ship, where it was lifted aboard in nets or slings and packed by hand into the hold. The work was slow and costly, and a cargo ship could spend nearly as much time in port as at sea. Theft and breakage were also common.

In April 1956 a converted wartime tanker, the Ideal X, sailed from Newark, New Jersey, to Houston, Texas, carrying fifty-eight metal containers on its deck. The voyage was organized by Malcom McLean, a trucking businessman. Shipping goods in large boxes was not a new idea; railways and some shipping lines had experimented with containers for decades. What McLean pursued was a whole system: boxes that moved from truck to ship and back without being unpacked, along with ships and cranes designed to handle them.

The system did not spread at once. Different companies built boxes of different sizes, which could not easily be stacked together or lifted by the same equipment. Beginning in the late 1960s, international standards fixed a small set of dimensions, most famously lengths of twenty and forty feet. Ports that invested in large container cranes grew, while many older docks closed, and the cost of loading cargo fell sharply.

Why does English say foot where Latin says pes, and three where Latin says tres? The answer lies in a set of regular sound changes described in the early nineteenth century. In 1818 the Danish scholar Rasmus Rask noted systematic correspondences between the Germanic languages, the family that includes English, German, and Gothic, and other languages such as Latin, Greek, and Sanskrit. In 1822 the German scholar Jacob Grimm, better known today for the folktales he collected with his brother, set them out in detail, and they came to be known as Grimm's law.

The central idea is that certain consonants of the ancestral language shifted in Germanic while they were largely kept elsewhere. Where Latin has p, t, and k, English typically has f, th, and h: pes and foot, tres and three, cornu and horn. These pairs are not borrowings but inherited words that changed along different paths. The pattern was regular enough that scholars could use it to identify related words that looked quite different on the surface.

The law had exceptions, however. Latin pater, for instance, corresponds to Gothic fadar, with a d where the law predicts a th sound. In 1875 the Danish linguist Karl Verner showed that such exceptions were themselves regular: the outcome depended on where the stress had fallen in the ancestral word, as Sanskrit, which kept the old stress, still showed. His discovery helped encourage the view that sound changes operate without exception, so that apparent irregularities point to rules not yet found.

When the first Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened in Washington State in July 1940, it had one of the longest suspension spans in the world, about 2,800 feet. It was also unusually slender. Its designer, Leon Moisseiff, had replaced the deep stiffening trusses then common beneath a suspension bridge's roadway with solid steel girders only eight feet deep. The result was light and cheaper to build, but the deck rose and fell noticeably in moderate winds, so often that local drivers nicknamed the bridge Galloping Gertie.

On November 7, 1940, in a steady wind of roughly forty miles per hour, the motion changed character. Instead of rising and falling, the deck began to twist, one side lifting as the other dropped. The twisting grew for about an hour until sections of the deck tore loose and fell into the water. The collapse is often described as resonance, the wind pushing the bridge at its natural rhythm like a child pumping a swing. Engineers now generally regard that account as too simple, since a steady wind has no rhythm to match. Instead, the twisting deck altered the airflow around itself in a way that fed energy back into the motion, a process known as flutter.

The failure changed bridge design. Engineers began routinely testing scale models of long-span bridges in wind tunnels, and the replacement bridge, opened in 1950, was built with a much deeper, open stiffening truss.
